Check a fit against the data it was fitted to

Source: R/check_fit.R
check_fit.Rd

Reports, per group of the predictor, the observed location and scale of the response against what the fitted model simulates, with a posterior predictive p-value for each. Sits alongside check_chains, which checks the sampler, and check_priors, which checks the priors: this checks the fit against the data.

check_fit(x, group = NULL, ndraws = 1000, seed = 10, ...)

# S3 method for class 'bayesnecfit'
check_fit(x, group = NULL, ndraws = 1000, seed = 10, ...)

# S3 method for class 'bayesmanecfit'
check_fit(x, group = NULL, ndraws = 1000, seed = 10, ...)

# S3 method for class 'bayesnechurdlefit'
check_fit(x, group = NULL, ndraws = 1000, seed = 10, combined = TRUE, ...)

Arguments

x

An object of class bayesnecfit or bayesmanecfit as returned by bnec.

group

A numeric vector of the same length as the data giving the group each row belongs to, or a single numeric giving the number of bins to cut the predictor into. If NULL (the default) the distinct values of the predictor are used where they are replicated, and the predictor is binned otherwise, with a warning.

ndraws

A numeric vector of length 1, the number of posterior draws to simulate from. Reduced silently to the number the fit actually holds where that is smaller.

seed

A numeric vector of length 1. Passed to set.seed before simulating, so the result is reproducible.

...

Unused.

combined

A logical vector of length 1. If TRUE (the default) a third table is returned checking the two components against the response they jointly predict, which is what the user actually observed. The growth component is predicted onto the full exposed set rather than onto its own data, since it is fitted on survivors only.

Value

A data.frame with one row per group (per model, for a bayesmanecfit), carrying the group, the number of observations, the observed and simulated mean and standard deviation, their ratios, a posterior predictive p-value for each, and a logical flag marking the control group. For the mixture families it also carries the observed and simulated proportion of zeros.

Details

Why this is not dispersion

dispersion reports one global statistic, and for any family with a free dispersion parameter that parameter absorbs exactly the discrepancy the global statistic measures. On the packaged manec_example the global Pearson ratio is 1.011, with a 95\ of 0.71 to 1.44 — a clean bill of health — while the same fit simulates about 27\ variability than the data show in the control region. A global summary is structurally incapable of showing that, which is why this check is local.

Why the control row matters

nsec sets its reference from the sig_val quantile of the posterior of the control mean, so the width of that posterior sets the reference. Overstate control variability and the reference falls, the curve crosses it later, and NSEC moves right — a less protective number. Understate it and NSEC moves left. A curve pulled away from the control data biases the same reference in location rather than spread. The control row is flagged for that reason.

Residuals, not raw values

The scale statistic is computed on residuals. Within a group the raw standard deviation of the response mixes residual variability with the slope of the curve across the group, which would make every steep-region group look overdispersed.

Model averaging does not protect you here

Stacking weights come from a global elpd. The control is a handful of rows out of many, so a candidate model can hold high weight while fitting the control badly — it wins on the bulk of the curve and pays almost nothing for the control. For a bayesmanecfit the per-model rows are therefore reported alongside the averaged rows, or the table could not say which model is doing the damage.

For a bayesnechurdlefit one table is returned per component, following the precedent dispersion sets. The two carry different response vectors — growth is fitted on survivors only, survival on every individual — so there is no single table that describes both.

See also

pp_check, dispersion, check_chains, check_priors

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
library(bayesnec)
nec4param <- pull_out(manec_example, model = "nec4param")
check_fit(nec4param)
} # }
